reason: The chambers need muscle to squeeze, so these pieces directly address the pump goal.
expectation: The muscle will surround the chambers and let them squeeze.

effect: The muscular chambers squeeze fluid in both directions, so they need a way to prevent backflow.
reaction: The two-way arrows make the purpose of the valves clear.
reason: The valve picture shows them closing against reverse flow, which should direct the squeeze forward.
expectation: The valves should prevent backflow through the chambers.

effect: The valves direct flow during squeezing and refill; the pump still needs repeated contractions.
reaction: The paired squeeze and refill panels make the valves' role clear.
reason: The pacemaker cells' spreading electrical wave suggests they can coordinate repeated heartbeats.
expectation: The pacemaker cells will trigger repeated squeezes that drive blood forward.

effect: The pacemaker completed the beating pump; the remaining goal is to connect it with blood and a returning vessel route.
reaction: The distinction between starting the beat and nerves adjusting it is useful.
reason: Hemoglobin has oxygen-binding sites, and the flexible envelopes appear to be the structure of red blood cells.
expectation: The hemoglobin will fit inside the envelopes to make oxygen-carrying red blood cells.

alternatives.reason: Those vessels also look like parts of the returning route.

effect: Hemoglobin and the envelopes made red blood cells, which can make ATP from sugar without mitochondria. Plasma is still available to make blood.
reaction: The contrast with the muscle cells is interesting.
reason: Red blood cells suspended in plasma should form blood for the returning route.
expectation: The red blood cells will join the plasma to make blood.

alternatives.reason: These also appear to be parts of the vessel route.

effect: The red cells and plasma formed oxygen-carrying blood, leaving the vessel route to assemble.
reaction: The picture clearly distinguishes hemoglobin inside the cells from sugar dissolved in plasma.
reason: Capillary networks should connect the outgoing arteries to the returning veins.
expectation: The vessels will form a route through capillaries and back toward the heart.

effect: The vessels now form a returning circuit with slots for the pump and transport medium.
reaction: The marked connections make the next fittings clear.
reason: The beating heart is the pump needed by the circuit.
expectation: The heart will fit into the pump slot.

alternatives.reason: The blood also appears to fit the transport medium slot.

effect: The beating heart now fills the circuit’s pump slot, leaving the transport medium to add.
reaction: The heart’s connections to outgoing and returning vessels make the circuit clearer.
reason: Oxygen-carrying blood fits the remaining transport medium slot.
expectation: The blood will fill the circuit and complete the returning route.

effect: Adding blood completed the circuit. The result shows oxygen and nutrients leaving capillaries for tissues while red blood cells remain inside, and blood returning to circulate again.
reaction: The tissue-exchange inset ties the circuit back to the muscle cells’ need for supplies.

mostWorthwhile.text: Fitting blood into the circuit was most worthwhile because it brought the pump, vessels and tissue supply together in one picture.

leastWorthwhile.text: Fitting the heart into the named pump slot was predictable, though it made the outgoing and returning connections clear.

surprise.text: I was interested that red blood cells make ATP from sugar in their fluid despite having no mitochondria.

arbitrary.text: No action felt especially arbitrary; the pictures and named slots gave each combination a clear purpose.

continue.text: I would choose to continue because I am curious how the body obtains the oxygen and nutrients that this circuit delivers. The chapter connected individual cell needs to a body-wide system clearly.
